name: Like a Roman
blurb: How Romans actually said things: greetings, manners and idioms, then questions and answers entirely in Latin.

units.title: Greetings and manners
units.blurb: Salvē, valē, thanks, please, names, and yes/no questions
units.intro: Romans greeted each other with _Salvē_ (to several people: _Salvēte_) and parted with _Valē_. Both are really commands: 'be well'. To ask how someone is, they said _Quid agis?_ (literally 'What are you doing?'). The ending -ne turns a statement into a yes/no question: _Fessusne es?_ = Are you tired? When you speak to someone by name, the name changes to the vocative: _Mārcus_ → _Mārce_. To say thanks, Romans said 'I give thanks to you': _Grātiās tibi agō_. In this unit you are often given a situation rather than an English sentence: say what a Roman would say.

units.title: How Romans say it
units.blurb: Age, liking, having, the hour: Latin's own way of saying things
units.intro: Latin often says things differently from English. 'I am twenty years old' is _Vīgintī annōs nātus sum_ ('I am born twenty years'). 'I like it' is _Mihi placet_ ('it is pleasing to me'): the thing you like is the subject and you are in the dative. 'I have a book' can be _Mihi liber est_ ('a book is to me'). 'I am cold' uses a verb: _frīgeō_. To ask the time, Romans said _Quota hōra est?_ ('Which hour is it?'). Don't translate word by word from English. Learn each pattern as a whole.

units.title: Latin only
units.blurb: Questions in Latin, answers in Latin
units.intro: From here on the questions are in Latin and you answer in Latin. Don't translate into English first. Spot the question word (_quis_ who, _quid_ what, _ubi_ where, _quota_ which) and the verb ending, then answer with the matching form: _edis_ ('you eat') is answered by _edō_ ('I eat'). The English appears only after you answer, in case you need it.
